source.title: Noise Stability Regularization for Improving BERT Fine-tuning
source.authors: Hang Hua; Xing-Jian Li; D. Dou; Chengzhong Xu; Jiebo Luo

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether explicit noise-stability regularization changes the natural-label training–evaluation gap, using BERT fine-tuning in few-sample NLP tasks.
record.gate_note: The paper directly compares generalization gaps with standard fine-tuning and LNSR. It does not test arbitrary or random-label memorization, width beyond interpolation, the listed architecture or optimizer comparisons, dropout, magnitude-aware sharpness, or removal of memorized examples. Noise-sensitivity results are recorded under fits_no_version because they do not measure V7's magnitude-aware sharpness.
record.test_reason: The study evaluates noise-stability regularization during BERT fine-tuning, but none of its own results test V1–V8. In particular, representation sensitivity to injected noise is different from V7's magnitude-scaled weight perturbations and ranking of generalization gaps.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that LNSR improves generalizability and stability in few-sample BERT fine-tuning, reporting smaller training–evaluation gaps, higher development scores, and lower seed variability than standard fine-tuning.
record.recipe_differences: Adds layer-wise noise-stability regularization during BERT fine-tuning; evaluates few-sample NLP tasks rather than the listed claim-version setups.
record.method_sensitivity: Noise-injection position: the text says performance does not fluctuate much across positions and all positions improve over vanilla fine-tuning; lower-layer injection usually gives relatively higher accuracy and stability.

fits_no_version.finding: Table 3 reports smaller training–evaluation score gaps with LNSR on all four tasks: RTE 25.76 to 17.41, MRPC 9.00 to 8.18, CoLA 36.25 to 30.09, and STS-B 8.93 to 8.22.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Layer-wise noise-stability regularization can reduce training–evaluation score gaps during few-sample BERT fine-tuning.

fits_no_version.finding: Figure 1 qualitatively associates higher MRPC accuracy with lower sensitivity of top-layer representations to noise injected into lower-layer outputs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Representation noise stability can be associated with held-out performance during BERT fine-tuning.

record.peer_reviewed: North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The reported generalization-gap comparison is limited to one BERT-Large model and four few-sample GLUE tasks. The text gives no uncertainty measure for Table 3's gaps.
record.rows_left_out: No qualifying results omitted. Other tables report development-set performance and seed variability, but not the training–evaluation gap measured in Table 3.

untested.parts: Coexistence of random-label fitting and natural-label generalization under the same architecture and recipe; chance-level random-label held-out performance.
Test-error behavior as width increases beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer comparisons and effects of tuning, switching optimizers, or decoupled weight decay.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Dropout interventions, small-data exceptions, excessive dropout, and interactions with augmentation or weight decay. Mixout is not a dropout experiment.
Magnitude-aware weight sharpness, its association with generalization gaps at similarly low training loss, and ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
Removal of examples selected by label-memorization influence versus equally sized random removals.

record.verdict_notes: Table 3 specifies 20 seeds, whereas the main performance tables specify 25. These results do not warrant verdicts on any listed version, and no omitted result in the supplied text tests one.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fit and held-out accuracy on natural labels.
Width sweep beyond interpolation and test-error behavior.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers.
Adaptive versus non-adaptive optimizer generalization comparisons.
Large- versus small-batch comparisons under fixed epoch budgets.
Dropout effects and its interaction with data augmentation or weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and comparisons with norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring test accuracy.
